course.title: AP World History: Modern
course.description: Understand the people, ideas, and connections that shaped the world from c. 1200 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Explore how states rose, belief systems spread, trade networks connected regions, and revolutions reshaped societies from c. 1200 to the present.

unit.title: Globalization
unit.description: Study how technology, disease, and environmental change reshaped the world, how the global economy and culture developed, and how people and institutions responded to globalization.

themes.title: Interactions of humans with the environment
themes.question: How did geography, crops, resources, or disease shape choices?
themes.example: Andean terraces made steep slopes more usable for farming.

themes.title: Social interactions and organization
themes.question: Who had status, opportunities, or obligations?
themes.example: Examination preparation favored families that could afford education.

themes.title: Political systems and governance
themes.question: How did rulers gain authority and administer territory?
themes.example: Song officials carried imperial decisions into local government.

themes.title: Economic systems
themes.question: How were goods produced, exchanged, taxed, or distributed?
themes.example: Mali drew revenue from commerce through its territory.

themes.title: Cultural developments and interactions
themes.question: How did beliefs, learning, and artistic practices influence society?
themes.example: Buddhist monasteries connected religious practice with education.

themes.title: Technology and innovation
themes.question: What techniques or tools changed what people could do?
themes.example: Inca roads and knotted records helped officials coordinate resources.

questions.prompt: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights of 1948 declared that
choices: only citizens of UN member states had rights
all people are equal in dignity and rights
rights depended on a person's religion
colonial rule was legal under international law
questions.explanation: It applied rights to all people regardless of race, sex, or religion.
choiceExplanations: It applied rights to all people regardless of race, sex, or religion.
Activists used it against colonial rule.
questions.distinguisher: UN members adopted it, but it applied to all people everywhere.

questions.prompt: India's constitution of 1950 addressed caste discrimination by
choices: making caste membership a legal requirement for jobs
abolishing untouchability and reserving places
banning Hindu temples from public life
reserving government jobs for upper castes
questions.explanation: Reservations opened education and jobs to lower castes.
choiceExplanations: Reservations opened education and jobs to lower castes.
Reserved places went to lower castes.
questions.distinguisher: Reserved government jobs went to lower castes, not upper castes.

questions.prompt: Liberation theology called on the Catholic Church to
choices: support military governments
work for justice for the poor
withdraw from politics entirely
end all missionary work
questions.explanation: Its supporters saw helping the poor as a religious duty.
choiceExplanations: Its supporters saw helping the poor as a religious duty.
It did not address missionary work.
questions.distinguisher: Liberation theology called for more political engagement, not less.

questions.prompt: India's caste reforms and China's response to Tiananmen Square differed in that
choices: both governments expanded citizens' rights
India extended rights; China used force
both governments used force against protesters
China's government extended voting rights
questions.explanation: One reformed through law; the other repressed protest.
choiceExplanations: One reformed through law; the other repressed protest.
China did not hold free elections.
questions.distinguisher: India extended rights, but China repressed the 1989 movement.

questions.prompt: The adoption of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948 is best understood in the context of
choices: the horrors of World War II and the Holocaust
the end of the Cold War and Soviet collapse
the scramble for Africa and colonial rule
the Protestant Reformation and religious wars
questions.explanation: The war's atrocities spurred efforts to define universal rights.
choiceExplanations: The war's atrocities spurred efforts to define universal rights.
The Cold War was beginning in 1948.
questions.distinguisher: The Declaration came at the start of the Cold War, not its end.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
choices: was binding international law for all states
was not binding but was cited by activists
applied only to women and children
was rejected by the United Nations
questions.explanation: Its moral authority gave activists a tool.
choiceExplanations: The passage says it was not binding.
Its moral authority gave activists a tool.
questions.distinguisher: The Declaration was influential but not binding law.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 9.5 key concept: rights-based discourses challenged old assumptions about race, class, gender, and religion
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing rights movements after 1945
stimulusBlocks.text:
In 1948, the United Nations adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, which declared that all people are born free and equal in dignity and rights, without distinction of race, sex, religion, or birth. It was not binding law, but activists around the world cited it.

Women's movements won the vote in most countries by the 1970s and pushed for equal access to education and work. In India, the 1950 constitution abolished untouchability and reserved places in universities and government jobs for members of the lowest castes.

questions.prompt: Women's movements and India's caste reforms described in the passage were similar in that both
choices: challenged inherited inequality
were led by the same people
began before 1900
were opposed by the United Nations
questions.explanation: Both sought equal access to education and work.
choiceExplanations: Both sought equal access to education and work.
questions.distinguisher: Women's suffrage campaigns began earlier, but the reforms described came after 1945.

questions.prompt: The passage best supports which argument about rights after 1945?
choices: Rights movements ended all discrimination
Ideas of universal rights challenged old hierarchies
Rights movements were limited to Europe
Governments rejected the idea of human rights
questions.explanation: Universal rights challenged race, gender, and caste hierarchies.
choiceExplanations: Universal rights challenged race, gender, and caste hierarchies.
questions.distinguisher: Rights movements challenged discrimination but did not end it.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, military governments in Latin America viewed liberation theology priests as
choices: allies
subversives
foreign agents of China
irrelevant
questions.explanation: They treated the priests as threats.
choiceExplanations: They treated the priests as threats.
The passage does not link them to China.
Romero's killing shows they were taken seriously.
questions.distinguisher: Romero's assassination shows governments took the movement seriously.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 9.5 key concept: movements for reform drew on religion and other traditions, and states responded in different ways
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing reform movements and state responses, 1960–1990
stimulusBlocks.text:
In Latin America in the 1960s and 1970s, some Catholic priests developed liberation theology, which taught that the church should work for social justice for the poor. Military governments often treated these priests as subversives, and in 1980 Archbishop Óscar Romero of El Salvador was assassinated while saying Mass.

In China in 1989, students gathered in Tiananmen Square to demand political freedom. The government declared martial law, and the army cleared the square by force.

questions.prompt: The events in the passage would best support which argument about responses to reform?
choices: Governments always accepted demands for reform
Reform movements avoided religion
Some governments used force against calls for change
Reform movements succeeded quickly everywhere
questions.explanation: Romero's assassination and Tiananmen show violent responses.
choiceExplanations: Romero's assassination and Tiananmen show violent responses.
questions.distinguisher: Some governments reformed, but those in the passage resisted.
